claims.text: Near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing at least six elements have sufficiently high configurational entropy to stabilize a single-phase solid solution at 773–1173 K.
Equimolar four-element nanoparticles undergo phase separation under conditions where six-element nanoparticles remain single-phase.
Both the four-element and six-element nanoparticle batches initially form approximately 10 nm single-phase solid solutions.
Changing an equimolar nanoparticle from four to six components increases its configurational entropy.
Configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase multi-element lattice.
The free energy of mixing is described by ΔG_mix = ΔH_mix − T·S_conf.
At elevated temperature, the T·S_conf contribution in the six-element system outweighs positive mixing enthalpies.
The resulting Gibbs-free-energy balance prevents phase separation in the six-element nanoparticles.
The lower configurational entropy of the four-element system makes separated phases thermodynamically favorable.
After aging at 973 K for 100 h under Ar, the six-element nanoparticles will retain one set of diffraction peaks and homogeneous elemental maps.
After the same aging treatment, the four-element nanoparticles will develop additional or split diffraction peaks and compositional segregation.
The proposed entropy-controlled behavior applies to equimolar nanoparticles approximately 5–15 nm in diameter in inert atmospheres at annealing temperatures of at least 773 K.
The proposed behavior may not apply to particles larger than 20 nm or to particles aged in reactive atmospheres.
The critical component count required for stabilization and the minimum time needed to reach equilibrium are unknown.
